w:r.w:t: A connected web and mobile system for quotations, invoicing and real-time field-work tracking, prepared for Ubuhlebethu Business Enterprise cc
This document is prepared for the management of Ubuhlebethu Business Enterprise cc to introduce Ubuhlebethu ConnectPro, a proposed web and mobile system designed to

the company's quotation, invoicing and site-progress-tracking processes. Ubuhlebethu is an established, award-winning construction company, operating across Gauteng, Free State, Mpumalanga, Limpopo and
, and currently runs these processes manually — through phone calls, WhatsApp messages, printed documents and department-specific spreadsheets.

The purpose of ConnectPro is to give clients a self-service portal to request and track quotations, give office and QS staff a single system for costing and invoicing, and give field workers and site managers a mobile tool to log work completed and track material usage in real time. This removes the current reliance on phone calls and disconnected paper
gives management a live view of project status without needing to contact each site individually.

This document sets out the requirements, analysis artifacts, architecture, data design, security approach, DevOps practices, running costs, and change-management plan for the system, and forms the basis on which the team will build and demonstrate the working prototype and, subsequently, the full implementation in Task 2 and Task 3 of this
ConnectPro is expected to reduce quotation turnaround time from days to hours and eliminate the administrative overhead of manual invoicing

Requirements were gathered through review of Ubuhlebethu's company profile and services, and through the current-state analysis conducted for the initial project proposal, which identified that the business relies entirely on manual, disconnected processes for client enquiries, quotations, invoicing and site reporting (see Section 2.

, project and end users, the team reviewed Ubuhlebethu's company profile (services offered, project history, and management/ownership structure) and mapped the company's current manual workflow from client enquiry through to on-site progress reporting. This confirmed that no dedicated business system currently exists, that records are kept separately by each department (QS, site managers, corporate affairs), and that field workers have no digital means of logging work completed while on site.

User stories are written in the standard format: As a [role], I want to [goal], so that [reason].
As a Client, I want to request a quotation online, so that I do not have to wait for a site visit before receiving a price indication.
As a Client, I want to view the status of my quotations and invoices in one place, so that I always know where my project stands.
As a Client, I want to ask a chatbot about my invoices and quotations in plain language, so that I get answers without phoning the office.
As Office/QS Staff, I want the system to suggest a draft cost estimate from the project scope, so that I have a faster starting point for costing.
As Office/QS Staff, I want to approve or reject a quotation and automatically generate an invoice on approval, so that invoicing is faster and less
As a Site Manager, I want to see real-time site reports and photos from my field workers, so that I do not have to phone the site for updates.
As a Site Manager, I want to assign tasks to field workers and monitor their completion status, so that I can ensure all site work is progressing according to schedule.
As a Field Worker, I want to log
and upload a photo from my phone, so that my progress is recorded without paperwork.
As a Field Worker, I want the app to automatically tag my site photo by construction stage, so that I do not have to manually
As a System Administrator, I want to deactivate a user account, so that access can be revoked when someone leaves a project or the company.
As a System Administrator, I want to view the audit trail of all user actions, so that I can investigate any unauthorized activity or data changes.

The following non-functional requirements were identified during a requirements-gathering and validation meeting with Ubuhlebethu management on 05 August 2026 via Microsoft Teams. The discussion focused on the organization’s day-to-day operational needs, expected system usage, user roles, AI functionality, security requirements and anticipated growth. These requirements define the quality, performance and operational constraints that the system must satisfy regardless of its specific functional features.

NFR-01 — Performance: Web pages and API endpoints must respond within 2 seconds under normal operating load. Core functions such as submitting quotations, viewing projects and recording site reports must remain usable without noticeable delays.

NFR-02 — Availability: The system should achieve a minimum of 99% uptime during business hours. The application must be hosted by using a managed cloud provider rather than relying on on-premises hardware, reducing the risk of service disruption caused by local infrastructure failures.

NFR-03 — Security: All data transmitted between users and the system must be encrypted using HTTPS/TLS. User passwords must be securely hashed, and server-side role-based access control (RBAC) must ensure that users can only access functions and information appropriate to their assigned role.

NFR-04 — Usability: The system must be simple enough for field workers to complete and submit a basic site report in under one minute on an Android mobile device, including the ability to upload a site photograph. The interface should minimize unnecessary steps because field workers may be operating on active construction sites.

NFR-05 — Scalability: The database and cloud infrastructure must support growth from approximately 100 users to at least 10,000 users without requiring a fundamental redesigning of the system architecture. The solution should therefore allow computing and database resources to be scaled as demand increases.

NFR-06 — AI Reliability: AI-powered features, including the Quotation Assistant, Chatbot and Natural-Language Search, must not prevent users from completing core business activities when the AI service is unavailable, slow or produces an unreliable response. If an AI request times out or returns a low-confidence result, the system must provide a manual or structured-search fallback within 3 seconds, allowing the user to continue with the task.

NFR-07 — Compliance: The system must process and store client and employee personal information in accordance with the requirements of the Protection of Personal Information Act (POPIA). Personal information must only be collected, accessed and retained for legitimate business purposes, with appropriate access controls applied.

NFR-08 — Maintainability: The application must use a layered architecture with clear separation of concerns between the presentation, business logic and data-access layers. This should allow individual features to be modified or extended without requiring large-scale rewrites of unrelated parts of the system.

NFR-09 — Compatibility: The web application must render and function correctly on the latest two versions of Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge and Safari. The Android mobile application must support Android 10 and later to accommodate the expected devices used by field workers.

NFR-10 — Localization: The system should initially support English and isiZulu, particularly for field-worker-facing functionality, while being designed so that additional South African official languages can be added as Ubuhlebethu expands its operations across different provinces. Language-specific interface text should therefore be separated from the application's core logic

A client's request first passes through the AI Service to generate a draft cost estimate, which is stored alongside the quotation in a Submitted state — it is never sent to the client automatically. QS staff review pending quotations, and approving one both updates its status and creates a linked Invoice record in the same transaction.
State diagram for a quotation's lifecycle

state when created by the AI Assistant or QS staff. From Draft, it moves to Submitted when the QS sends it to the client for review. If the client requests changes, it returns to Draft for revision. Upon client acceptance, it transitions to Approved, which automatically triggers invoice generation. Once invoiced, the quotation moves to Invoiced and is considered complete. From the Submitted

, the quotation may also transition directly to Closed if it expires without client action, or to Rejected if the client declines the proposal. Additionally, if the QS determines that a quotation needs further internal refinement after submission, it can be moved back to Under Review and subsequently returned to Draft for amendments. Terminal states include Closed, Rejected, and Invoiced; no further transitions are permitted from these states. Guard conditions enforce that only allowed state changes
example, a quotation cannot transition directly from Submitted to Invoiced without first passing through Approved.
For formal UML traceability, the permitted transitions are treated as guarded transitions. Examples

Draft → Submitted [QS sends quotation]; Submitted → Draft [client requests changes]; Submitted → Approved [client accepts quotation]; Submitted → Closed [quotation expires]; Submitted → Rejected [client declines]; and Approved → Invoiced [invoice created successfully]. These guards prevent invalid lifecycle transitions and are enforced by the quotation service.

The system is deployed as three logical nodes: a web/API host running the ASP.NET Core application, a managed database server, and external calls to Google's Gemini API for AI features. The mobile app is distributed as an installable APK for demonstration and does not require its own server — it communicates with the same hosted API as the web application.

The deployment view treats the Web Server, Database Server, Google Gemini API, File Storage, Client/Office Browser and Field Worker Android Device as deployable nodes/devices. Communication paths are explicitly labelled with HTTPS/REST or TLS, and the mobile device is included as a client node because it consumes the same hosted API as the web application.
Rollout strategy: deploy to a staging environment first, run smoke tests against the auth, quotation and AI endpoints, then
production via the CD pipeline described in Section 11.
Rollback: the previous container image / build artifact is retained so a failed deployment can be reverted within minutes.
Environment separation: development, staging and production each use separate database instances and separate API keys, configured through environment variables.

The system uses a relational database (SQL Server via Azure SQL, with EF Core as the ORM). This choice was made because the core data — clients, quotations, invoices, projects and users — has clearly defined relationships and benefits from enforced foreign-key integrity, ACID transactions (particularly important when a quotation approval must atomically create an invoice), and mature tooling for migrations. EF Core's Code-First migrations give the team a version-controlled history of schema changes, satisfying the requirement to track schema evolution rather than manually creating tables.

The domain model's six distinct role classes—Client, OfficeStaff,

, FieldWorker, Management, and SystemAdmin—are consolidated into a single Users table in the ERD with a Role discriminator column. This represents a deliberate single-table-per-hierarchy (STPH) inheritance mapping strategy, chosen because all role types share core authentication fields (

) and differ only in role-specific attributes that are sparsely populated across records. STPH simplifies authentication logic by allowing ASP.NET Core Identity to query a single table for credential verification, role claim retrieval, and RBAC permission checks, rather than performing costly
or polymorphic unions across six separate tables. Role-specific attributes are accommodated through nullable columns—for example,

only to Management—with application-layer validation ensuring that only permitted roles access or modify their designated fields. This approach also streamlines audit trail queries (since every user action logs a single numeric

) and simplifies reporting dashboards that aggregate user metrics across all roles without complex table unions. While STPH introduces some nullable columns and requires careful business-logic enforcement, these trade-offs are acceptable given the relatively low number of role-specific attributes per type and the substantial performance and maintainability benefits gained for authentication and authorization workflows, which are invoked on nearly every API request.

The system follows a layered (N-tier) architecture combined with a REST API, keeping presentation, business logic and data layers separate. This was chosen over a monolithic MVC-only approach because it lets both the web application and the Kotlin mobile app consume the same backend through a single, documented API, rather than duplicating business logic in two places.
: Layered architecture — presentation, business logic and data layers

The web application, backend API and database are hosted on Azure, using Azure App Service for the API, Azure SQL Database for the relational data, and Azure Blob Storage for site photos. The API sits in an application subnet reachable from the internet over HTTPS (port 443), while the database sits in a private/managed network reachable only from the API over TLS-encrypted TCP (port 1433).

The ASP.NET Core MVC web application and REST API are hosted on Azure App Service. The web application uses Razor Views for server-side page rendering, while the REST API provides a shared backend interface consumed by both the web application and Kotlin Android mobile application.

Security risk analysis complements the technical controls below. The following register identifies representative threats, their assessed likelihood and impact, and the corresponding mitigation strategy:
All client-to-server communication uses HTTPS/TLS. Database connections are encrypted using TLS, and insecure HTTP traffic is redirected or rejected where applicable.

Server-side authorization checks verify ownership and role permissions for every protected resource. Record IDs alone never grant access.
RBAC is enforced server-side using role claims and authorization policies. Administrative functions are restricted to
roles, and client-side controls cannot bypass API authorization.
Short-lived access tokens, refresh-token rotation, secure Android Keystore storage and server-side token validation. Revocation is supported when a session or account is compromised.
Login rate limiting, temporary account lockout, monitoring of repeated failed attempts and strong password requirements. Suspicious authentication activity is logged.
Anti-forgery tokens are applied to state-changing web forms. API authentication uses authorization headers for mobile requests, reducing classic cookie-based CSRF exposure.
Restrict permitted file types and sizes, validate MIME type and file signatures, generate safe filenames, store uploads outside executable application directories and scan or reject suspicious files.

API responses expose only fields required by the requesting role. Sensitive information is protected by authorization rules. Secrets and credentials are never written to logs. HTTPS/TLS protects data in transit.

Rapid, reliable delivery is treated as a first-class requirement, not an afterthought. The team uses GitHub for version control with a simple
-style branching model: feature branches are created
develop, merged via Pull Request after at least one team member's review, and develop is periodically merged into main to trigger a release.
GitHub Actions branching and CI/CD workflow
On every Pull Request into develop, the GitHub Actions pipeline automatically restores NuGet dependencies, builds the solution in Release configuration, and runs the full
test suite (covering 300+ tests across Controllers, Services, and Repositories) while enforcing a minimum code coverage of 80% via Coverlet; it also runs

for any front-end JavaScript/TypeScript changes, blocking the merge if any test fails or coverage drops below the threshold. On every merge into main, a second workflow builds a Docker container image tagged with the commit SHA, deploys it to the staging environment, runs smoke tests against the auth, quotation, and AI endpoints, and promotes to production only if all smoke tests pass—while retaining the previous container image to enable instant rollback in under five minutes. As part of this pipeline, fallback behavior for AI features is built and tested: if a call to Gemini times out or returns a low-confidence result, the backend stores the request unclassified and flags it for manual review, ensuring that a slow or failed AI response never blocks core user actions like submitting a quotation or logging a site report.

Ubuhlebethu currently serves clients across five provinces with no digital system, so early adoption is expected to be gradual. The team projects roughly 100 active users (clients, office staff and field workers combined) within the first three months, growing to around 1,000 by the end of year one as more site teams and repeat clients are onboarded, and towards 5,000–10,000 by the end of year two if the system is rolled out company-wide and offered to a wider client base. Costs scale from free-tier (R0/month) at launch to an estimated R4,300/month at 10,000 users — a cost the company can offset against the reduced admin time and faster invoicing cycle the system is designed to deliver.

The adoption timeline (approximately 100 active users in the first three months, around 1,000 by the end of year one, and 5,000–10,000 by the end of year two) is a planning assumption informed by the client discussion held on 05 August 2026 and should be validated with management during Task 2. Where the client has not supplied a specific adoption figure, the team treats the value as an estimate rather than a confirmed commitment.
